extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO disciplinary counsel, and respondents in USPTO OED proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative criteria used by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline and an Administrative Law Judge to determine practitioner misconduct and appropriate sanctions in disciplinary proceedings under 37 C.F.R. and 35 U.S.C. § 32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely answer Complaint / default consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.36 of Title 37 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets forth the requirement for answering the Complaint and the consequences for not doing so: 'Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If respondent does not file a timely answer (often required within the time stated in the Complaint or Notice of Hearing), the factual allegations are deemed admitted and default judgment may be entered; the decision may adopt the Complaint's allegations as findings of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to notify OED of change of postal address
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a) requires a registered practitioner to provide written notice to the OED Director of any change in his or her postal address within 30 days of the date of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to update the official address can result in mailed disciplinary correspondence being effective and returned mail does not excuse noncompliance; certified mail to address of record is valid service (document cites certified-mail deliveries and signed receipts).

rubrics_metrics.name: OED burden of proof (clear and convincing evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must prove any affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence as well. The decision applies this standard to admitted facts (default).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to discipline practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has the 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' 35 U.S.C. § 32 allows suspension or exclusion if a person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates Office regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for imposing discipline (suspension/exclusion); the panel evaluates whether violations meet these statutory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a), (b) via § 10.23(c)(8) — duty to inform client of Office correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.23(a) and (b) via § 10.23(c)(8) proscribes failing to inform a client of correspondence received from the Office when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client or former client, and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to failure to notify clients of Ex Parte Quayle actions, Non-Final Office Actions, Requirements for Restriction/Election, Notices of Abandonment, Notices of Allowance, and other communications—i.e., any Office correspondence that could materially affect the client’s matter should be communicated to client in a timely fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglect of legal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.77(c) proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: failing to prosecute patent applications, allowing applications to become abandoned without client knowledge/consent, and failing to take required steps in trademark prosecutions. Neglect supports discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2) — failing to carry out contract of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.84(a)(2) proscribes intentionally failing to carry out a contract of employment entered into with a client for professional services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where practitioner accepted advance fees, agreed to perform prosecution work, but intentionally failed to report Office communications, allowed abandonments, or otherwise failed to perform contracted services.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.23(b)(4) proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting the status of an application to a client (e.g., telling client 'USPTO is slow' or 'nothing yet' when application had been abandoned) is conduct violating this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i) — giving false or misleading information to a client
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.23(c)(2)(i) proscribes knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with any business before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 10.23(b)(4); knowingly false statements about application status to clients are violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.40(a) — improper withdrawal and failure to refund unearned fees
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.40(a) proscribes withdrawing from employment without permission of the Office, without giving due notice to his client, and without refunding promptly any part of a fee paid in advance that has not been earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning clients without notice to clients or USPTO and failing to refund unearned advance fees violates this rule; prompt refund upon termination or withdrawal is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(4) — failing to pay client funds promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: § 10.112(c)(4) proscribes failing to promptly pay the client funds in the possession of the practitioner which the client is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must return unearned fees and client funds held; failure to do so supports discipline and restitution orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.103 proscribes failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to failure to timely prosecute matters (e.g., failing to respond to Office Actions, failing to file substitute specimens) and general lack of diligence in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.104(a)(3) proscribes failing to keep the client reasonably informed about the status of a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must inform clients of significant developments; failure to notify clients of Notices of Allowance, Office Actions, abandonments, or registration issuance is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4) — promptly comply with client requests for information
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.104(a)(4) proscribes failing to promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failure to answer telephone calls, emails, or other client inquiries about case status is conduct violating this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d) — promptly deliver client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.115(d) proscribes failing to promptly deliver to the client any funds that the client is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must promptly deliver refunds and client funds; not doing so violates this rule (applied to unearned fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d) — refund advance payment upon termination
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.116(d) proscribes failing to refund any advance payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred upon termination of the practitioner-client relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon termination of representation, unearned advanced fees must be returned; failing to refund after abandonment is grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c) — disobeying tribunal obligations (restitution orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.304(c) proscribes knowingly disobeying an obligation under the rules of a tribunal except for an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes failing to pay restitution ordered by a court or disciplinary tribunal; refusing or ignoring tribunal orders to make restitution is an aggravating violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.505 proscribes engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner who is suspended or not admitted in any state must not represent clients before the Office; filing trademark applications or representing clients while suspended constitutes unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) — failing to cooperate with OED investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.801(b) proscribes knowingly failing to cooperate with OED in an investigation of any matter before it and knowingly failing to respond to lawful demands for information from a disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to lawfully issued RFIs, Lack of Response letters, or Supplemental RFIs (certified mail and e-mail attempts documented) constitutes noncooperation and a separate violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — dishonesty/fraud/misrepresentation toward clients or Office
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.804(c) proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct such as practicing while suspended, falsely holding oneself out as authorized, or not informing clients of suspension is a violation under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.804(d) proscribes conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include refusing to respond to OED RFIs despite ample notice and opportunity—such obstruction harms the disciplinary process and supports more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f) — OED authority to issue Requests for Information and Evidence (RFI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED may issue Requests for Information and Evidence pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f) to obtain information about a practitioner's conduct and licensure status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RFIs must be responded to within the time given (e.g., 30 days); certified-mail delivery to address of record constitutes lawful service; failure to respond can be charged as noncooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors per 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to client, public, legal system, or profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision references ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions (2005) for identifying aggravating/mitigating factors; aggravators include multiple violations, pattern of misconduct, bad-faith obstruction, lack of remorse, and failure to make restitution—these support more severe sanctions (e.g., exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex Parte Quayle (MPEP § 714.14) — condition for allowance except formal objections
rubrics_metrics.description: An Ex Parte Quayle is issued by the USPTO when an application is in condition for allowance except for formal objections, which typically include minor and obvious corrections. See MPEP § 714.14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an Ex Parte Quayle issues, replacement drawings or minor corrections may be required within a short period; failure to act on such correspondence can lead to abandonment—practitioner must notify client and act promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to file timely answers per procedural rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint filed pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2)(i) notifies respondent of requirement to file a written answer within the time stated (Complaint here advised respondent to file within 30 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance (timely answering, seeking extensions when appropriate) is required; failing to do so can lead to default and admission of allegations.
